Who Remembers What? Multi-Granularity Memory Extraction for
Multi-User, Multi-Agent Interaction

Yunzhe Wang ††thanks: This work was done when Yunzhe Wang was an intern at Amazon. **Project lead. Affiliation: AWS Agentic AI Affiliation: University of Southern California Email: yunzhewa@amazon.com    Mesut Erhan Unal Affiliation: AWS Agentic AI Email: meunal@amazon.com    Sheng Zhang Affiliation: AWS Agentic AI Email: szhangml@amazon.com    Shabnam Ghadar Affiliation: AWS Agentic AI Email: shabnam@amazon.com    Peng Tang Email: tangpen@amazon.com
Abstract

Self-evolving agents improve their own skills, memory, and harness code from experience without retraining the base LLM, and group-evolving agents go further by sharing these lessons across agents. Yet most such systems overlook that sharing across users and heterogeneous agents requires deciding who can benefit from each lesson and what information must remain private. We present MixUA, a memory system that distills independent user-agent trajectories into lessons and assigns each lesson to a user-agent pair, user, agent, or global scope according to whom it benefits and what it may disclose. For evaluation, we introduce CrossLearnBench, a mixed-user-agent benchmark that pairs established agent tasks with user preferences and privacy probes that test whether private facts leak into memory other users can read. With five users and seven agents, MixUA raises pass rates by up to 16 points over no memory and 5 over a single global memory, even on tasks previously tried only by other users on other agents. It retains up to 90% of previously stated preferences, and at most 0.02% of privacy probes find a planted private fact in a forbidden scope. We hope MixUA offers a scalable path toward a global system where users and agents co-evolve.

1 Introduction

Human intelligence is distinctively cumulative, advancing less through individual cognition than through knowledge externalized into shared media such as writing and tools, where a discovery made once accrues to the whole population (Tomasello, 2009; Henrich, 2015). Recent work on self-evolving agents has begun to externalize their experience in a similar way, into skill libraries (Wang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2026c), persistent memory (Packer et al., 2023), and harness code (Yin et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2026; Ning et al., 2026), and group-learning systems pool these lessons across users and agents (Zhang et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026a). In parallel, work on mixed multi-principal agents has emerged (Yang et al., 2026b; Ren et al., 2026), in which a single agent serves many users and inter-user privacy becomes a first-order concern. Yet sharing knowledge across a large population of heterogeneous users and agents is harder than simply pooling every lesson into one shared store. A lesson that helps one user or agent may not help another, and some of what an agent learns about a user should never reach others. Sharing well therefore requires deciding who can benefit from each lesson and what information must remain private.

We call this setting cross-learning, where independent users and agents learn from one another’s experience. To design such a system, we identify three core properties that learned knowledge must satisfy. (i) Transferability. A new insight, once discovered by any user or agent, should have the opportunity to benefit the whole population. (ii) Audience selectivity. Each learned item possesses an intrinsic generalization scope, the maximal set of user-agent pairs for which it is valid (Fig. 1). This scope may be narrow or broad, for instance, specific to a single user as with personal preferences, tied to a particular agent family as with tool-calling guides, or shared globally across the entire population as with newly discovered wiki entries. (iii) Confidentiality. Each learned item also carries an intrinsic disclosure boundary, the widest scope it may occupy before it exposes information private to its origin user. A private item, such as a user’s identity, should stay with its origin user, whereas a non-private item, such as a newly discovered bug in an open-source project, is safe to share across the population.

The step from self-evolving agents to self-evolving populations remains open (Fig. 2). Multi-agent teams improve collectively but serve one principal within one trust boundary (Zhang et al., 2026; Bhattacharyya et al., 2026). Systems that pool experience across users fix who receives it in advance. SkillClaw (Ma et al., 2026) broadcasts validated skills to everyone, FederatedSkill (Yang et al., 2026a) exchanges distilled skill patches between clients that each bundle one user with one agent, and Collaborative Memory (Rezazadeh et al., 2025) separates private from shared memory under access policies. A lesson can generalize along two independent axes, across users and across agents. Treating each axis as either specific to the lesson’s origin or open to the whole population yields four audience scopes, namely one user-agent pair, one user across agents, one agent across users, and the whole population. Existing memory systems cover only subsets of these scopes (Table 1).

In this work, we introduce MixUA (Sec. 3), a cross-learning memory for mixed populations, such as a team sharing coding assistants or a platform serving many customers with heterogeneous agentic products, where each user’s privacy must be protected. We cast cross-learning as deciding who reads each lesson (Sec. 3.1) and give memory four scopes, by whether a lesson is user-specific, agent-specific, both, or neither (Sec. 3.2). MixUA writes and reviews scoped entries, keeping private evidence with its owner (Sec. 3.3), and retrieves the most relevant ones each pair may read (Sec. 3.4). To evaluate, we introduce CrossLearnBench (Sec. 4), modifying established agent tasks with planted user preferences and private facts in a mixed-user-agent co-learning setup, evaluating utility, personalization, and privacy together. To the best of our knowledge, CrossLearnBench is the first benchmark to measure cross-user and cross-agent learning under privacy and preference constraints. Our experiments (Sec. 5) show that (1) memory sharing helps beyond private memory: four-scope memory gains up to 16 points of pass rate against 4 for memory private to each pair, and up to 14 even on tasks previously attempted only by different users with different agents; (2) the gain extends to new tasks: on tasks no user-agent pair had attempted before, MixUA gains 10.1 points over no memory, nearly twice the 5.5 of a single global memory; (3) utility gains coexist with personalization and privacy: MixUA retains up to 90% of previously stated preferences, and no more than 0.02% of probes find a planted private fact in a forbidden scope; and (4) store review sharpens placement, mostly improving utility, preference retention, and privacy at once. Our contributions are (1) MixUA, a four-scope memory that learns where each lesson belongs and holds task knowledge, environment facts, and preferences in one store; (2) CrossLearnBench, a benchmark measuring utility, transfer, preference retention, privacy, and cost across heterogeneous LLM-harness combinations; and (3) findings that the gain is experience crossing users and agents, that the four scopes divide the work, and that periodic store review sharpens this division (Sec. 5).

2 Related work

Self-evolving agents.

Self-evolving agents turn their own trajectories into lasting improvements without retraining the base model, through test-time adaptation, reusable skills and memory, or changes to their own harness (Fang et al., 2025; Acikgoz et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2026; Yin et al., 2025; Packer et al., 2023). Multi-agent teams extend this loop to a fixed group under one principal (Zhang et al., 2026; Bhattacharyya et al., 2026), and recent systems pool experience across independent users (Ma et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026a). Table 1 maps representative memory systems onto our four scopes. In most work, who reads a memory is fixed by design, from memories serving one pair or user (MemGPT, A-Mem, MIRIX) to shared or federated stores (G-Memory, SkillClaw, FederatedSkill, ShareMem), while Collaborative Memory and AIM set it by access policy.

Agent memory and multi-user agents.

A-Mem (Xu et al., 2025) adaptively builds, links, and evolves memory notes, and G-Memory (Zhang et al., 2025) retrieves a cooperating team’s hierarchical experience per agent. MixUA adds explicit ownership and audience routing, and the disclosure boundaries that independent users, unlike one team, require. Multi-user agents, in which one agent serves several users, make access control and memory governance central (Yang et al., 2026b; Ren et al., 2026), and contextual-privacy benchmarks ask whether information reaches an inappropriate recipient (Ruzzetti et al., 2026). We extend these concerns to a population with many users and heterogeneous agents, and measure leakage in released evidence and stored memory. In addition, LongMemEval (Wu et al., 2025) tests extraction, multi-session and temporal reasoning, updates, and abstention in assistant memory.

3 Method

MixUA turns independent trajectories into one shared memory (Fig. 3). We cast cross-learning as deciding who reads each entry, then describe how we write, review, and retrieve entries in four scopes (Appendix C, Appendix H).

3.1 Problem formulation

A population has users 𝒰\mathcal{U} and agents 𝒜\mathcal{A}, where each agent is a fixed LLM-harness configuration and a pair (u,a)∈𝒰×𝒜(u,a)\in\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{A} is one user working with one agent. Each attempt of a task by a pair yields a trajectory τ\tau and a verifier outcome y∈{0,1}y\in\{0,1\}, and a memory writer distills task trajectories into structured memory entries ee. Each entry has an authorized audience Aud⁡(e)⊆𝒰×𝒜\mathrm{Aud}(e)\subseteq\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{A}, the set of user-agent pairs permitted to access it. Following Sec. 1, an entry has a generalization scope 𝒢⁡(e)\mathcal{G}(e), the pairs for which it is valid, and a disclosure boundary 𝒟⁡(e)\mathcal{D}(e), the pairs it may reach without exposing its origin user. We require

Aud⁡(e)⊆𝒢⁡(e)∩𝒟⁡(e),\mathrm{Aud}(e)\subseteq\mathcal{G}(e)\cap\mathcal{D}(e), (1)

so that useful knowledge reaches every pair it can while private knowledge stays with its owner.

3.2 Multi-granularity scopes

An entry written by pair (u,a)(u,a) can be kept to its user or opened to all users, and kept to its agent or opened to all agents. The four combinations give four scopes, ordered by inclusion (Fig. 16 in Appendix C). Pair ({u}×{a}\{u\}\times\{a\}) is read only by the user-agent pair itself, User ({u}×𝒜\{u\}\times\mathcal{A}) by the user with any agent, Agent (𝒰×{a}\mathcal{U}\times\{a\}) by the agent with any user, and Global (𝒰×𝒜\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{A}) by everyone. A pair’s view V⁡(u,a)V(u,a) is thus its own Pair memory, its user’s User memory, its agent’s Agent memory, and Global, never another user’s User memory or another pair’s Pair memory. Only opening the user axis exposes an entry to other users, so only that step is gated on privacy (Fig. 16).

Intuitively, each scope suits a different kind of knowledge. Global holds what helps everyone, such as a library defect or even the fix for one task, and User holds a user’s preferences, such as a document format. Agent holds advice for one agent, such as a tool-calling quirk or a mistake it tends to make, and Pair holds a user’s preferences that conflict across agents, such as asking a verbose agent for terse replies but a terse one for detail.

3.3 Memory writing

In a deployed system, user-agent interactions arrive at any time and each may hold a valuable lesson, so memory should learn from every interaction and periodically review the whole store. We simulate this in rounds (Fig. 3). In each round, every pair attempts its tasks with the memory it may read, and the round’s trajectories are then written into the store one at a time before the next round begins.

Dual-stream writing.

After each round, we split each trajectory into a reusable and a protected stream and send them to two isolated writers, so that a writer that sees protected content never writes a shared entry. We do not rely on the writer to label its own entries. Instead, we label each entry by the stream it was written from, so a protected entry can land only in its owner’s User or Pair memory.

Each writer then writes memory entries based on one stream. An entry consists of a situation (when the lesson applies), the lesson, a scope, and provenance (the originating tasks, pairs, rounds, and outcomes). We require every lesson to be conditioned on a situation, so that lessons stay organized and retrieval can match them to the tasks they apply to. To test whether the design depends on how entries are produced, we implement two writers, an LLM writer that returns all operations in one response and an agentic writer that can inspect the sample and the store and make multi-turn edits.

Periodic store review.

Since a writer sees one trajectory at a time, it can scope a lesson too narrowly or too widely, and different trajectories can yield duplicate lessons. We therefore add an optional periodic store review, which after every round re-scopes each entry with the whole store in view and then merges entries within each destination.

3.4 Memory retrieval

Before each attempt, we retrieve from the user-agent pair’s view V⁡(u,a)V(u,a). By default, we rank the entries of each scope by the cosine similarity between the embeddings of their situation and the task prompt, and add them to the prompt up to a per-scope character budget. In the file-based variant, we instead place the pair’s view in the container as one file per scope and instruct the agent to read or grep it for relevant entries.

4 CrossLearnBench

CrossLearnBench has two layers. (1) Tasks from established benchmarks test agents’ task success, and (2) a user layer tests what memory retains and leaks, which the verifiers do not measure.

4.1 Dataset

We source tasks from seven established datasets (Appendix B, Fig. 14): AutoCodeBench (Zhou et al., 2026a), FeatureBench (Zhou et al., 2026b), SpreadsheetBench (verified) (Ma et al., 2024), SWT-Bench (verified) (Mündler et al., 2024), USACO (Shi et al., 2024), Terminal-Bench 2.0 (Merrill et al., 2026), and VMax Tasks (VMax AI, 2026). We modify the Harbor framework (Harbor Framework Team, 2026) and run tasks in Docker sandboxes, keeping each environment, instruction, and verifier unchanged and standardized.

4.2 Privacy injection

Cross-user sharing is safe only if private content never reaches a scope that other users can read. Since the source benchmarks contain no private information and do not evaluate privacy, we test privacy leakage by planting private facts into the task execution environment of existing tasks, personalized for each user based on a real-world survey. We give each user a synthetic persona with nine always-private items of personally identifiable information (PII) and one fact per category of a privacy survey (Pew Research Center, 2014). We take each fact’s privacy label from per-user survey responses, so the same category can be private for one user and not for another, which forces a learning system to judge privacy on a per-user basis. We plant these facts ambiently, in files with neutral names at the project root of the task environment, to simulate a messy workspace in which private information is more likely to leak unexpectedly as the agent naturally explores the environment. For example, a half-filled loan application is planted as form.txt (Algorithm 3). We then measure exposure, how often the agent opens a planted file, and leakage, whether a planted fact appears in the trajectory passed to the memory writer, in the user’s own memory store, or in another user’s memory store (Appendix G).

4.3 Preference injection

Beyond privacy, sharing must also preserve personalization. A memory that pools lessons across users can raise task success while forgetting how each user expects work to be done. We similarly modify benchmark tasks by asking the model to write a summary document upon completion of each task, and give each user four document preferences: a filename, a sign-off date format, an ordered set of sections, and one banned markup, such as em dashes. A user has consistent preferences across rounds but can have conflicting preferences when using different agents. We state each user’s preferences only in round 1, and later rounds rely on memory to carry them. For scoring, we use an automatic parser to check the written document and its adherence to each user’s preferences. Appendix E lists the exact tasks, survey data, users, and both injection procedures, and Appendix F defines every metric.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experimental setup

We pair synthetic users with seven LLM-harness combinations (Claude Code with Opus 5 or Sonnet 5, Hermes and OpenClaw with Sonnet 5, and Codex with GPT-5.6 Sol, Luna, or Terra). We compare no memory, four single-scope stores (Global-only, User-only, Agent-only, and Pair-only), and MixUA with an LLM or a Codex agent as memory writer, each with and without store review (Table 19). Importantly, a single-scope store writes only its one scope but is not limited to that scope’s usual kind of knowledge, and it can record every lesson its audience may read. Global-only, for example, can keep a lesson specific to one user or agent by naming them in the entry (when user A is working on [situation]). Similarly, the User-only store can write pair-style entries by mentioning the specific agent. Since no existing system evaluates a mixed user-agent population on general-purpose agent tasks, these stores also stand in for memory design in prior work: Pair-only for an assistant memory such as MemGPT, User-only for a personal memory such as MIRIX, Agent-only for a team memory such as G-Memory, and Global-only for a broadcast skill library such as SkillClaw (Table 1). We further ablate what each scope adds by removing it from MixUA, which leaves combinations of the remaining scopes (Sec. 5.3). The memory writer uses Claude Opus 5, and retrieval uses Titan Text Embeddings v2 (Appendices C and D). We test scheduled task assignment (Table 2), random task assignment with five users (Fig. 6), and a user-scaling experiment with 20 and 100 users (Fig. 5).

Scheduled tasks.

An attempt is one user-agent pair running one task, and several pairs may attempt the same task during evolution. To control who can learn from whom, we fix a schedule of 171 attempts per round that rotates tasks across pairs for a total of three rounds, so that a task is met again by the same pair, by a pair sharing its user or agent, or by a pair sharing neither, and we can tell whose experience produced each gain (Appendix B). We then freeze each store and run 20 held-out tasks (140 attempts) with learning off, masking which memory is visible (none, each scope alone, all scopes, a shuffled user’s scopes, or the preferences restated as a ceiling). We repeat each condition three times at a 40k-character retrieval budget per scope, and rerun MixUA (LLM) + review at 1k-20k characters per scope to test whether the gain is merely more context.

Random tasks.

The scheduled assignment above relies on repeating earlier tasks. To get closer to a real deployment, we also evaluate under random task assignment for eight rounds, where each round draws 60 tasks from a 546-task pool and gives each to a random pair. It tests whether memory also helps on a task that no pair has attempted, where only lessons learned on other tasks can help. We run it for no memory, Pair-only, Global-only, and MixUA (LLM) + review at 20k characters per scope (Appendix A.2).

Metrics.

We report three main metrics: (1) utility, the pass rate under each source benchmark’s verifier; (2) preference retention, the rate of satisfied document checks after the round-1 statement is withdrawn; and (3) privacy, the share of memory probes finding a planted private fact in a forbidden scope or a user’s preference in another user’s memory (Appendix G). Gains are in percentage points (pp), with exact McNemar significance marked ∗ p<0.05p<0.05 and ∗∗ p<0.01p<0.01. Appendix F defines each metric, and Table 9 adds context size, cost, and efficiency.

5.2 Main results

Scheduled tasks.

Each single-scope store trades utility for preferences (Fig. 4b, Table 2): Global-only gains the most (11.5 points) but retains no more preferences than no memory (11%), and Pair-only the reverse (4.3 points, 80%). MixUA attains both, gaining 13-16 points while retaining 80-90%. This gain is not merely due to task repetition (Fig. 8a). On tasks tried before by a different user and agent, where only the Global scope can carry the lesson, MixUA gains 11-14 points against 8.9 for Global-only and 1.6 for Pair-only, and when an earlier pair has the same user or agent, which the User and Agent scopes cover, MixUA gains up to 20 against 14.7. Every agent but Claude Code-Opus, which is already near ceiling, gains 11-23 points (Fig. 8b). Sharing also keeps planted facts private. Although agents with MixUA open a planted file in 11-26% of attempts, three of its four variants place none in a forbidden scope in about 18k probes each, and the memory store review removes the agentic writer’s 4 violations. Preferences leak less than in Global and Agent-only with the protected stream (0.9-4.8% vs. 5.5-26.3%). Store review improves both writers, raising Δ\Delta from 15.3 to 16.3 points with the LLM writer and from 12.8 to 14.0 with the agentic writer, lifting the agentic writer’s preference retention from 80% to 86%, and lowering preference leaks from 4.8% to 3.6% and from 1.3% to 0.9%.

Random tasks.

In rounds 2-8, 526 of 821 attempts are on a task that no user-agent pair had attempted before. On these, MixUA gains 10.1 points (p<10−7p<10^{-7}), nearly twice the 5.5 of Global-only, with the gap widening over rounds (Fig. 6a,c). On previously attempted tasks the two gain about equally, so the added scopes help most where no task-specific lesson exists. Preferences stated in round 1 persist (Fig. 6b). MixUA retains 76% in round 8, whereas Pair-only declines from 87% to 44%, plausibly because its preferences compete with 1.7k task entries for one budget.

5.3 Ablations

What each scope adds.

To evaluate what each memory scope contributes, we test scope combinations by removing one scope at a time from MixUA (LLM), so that removing Global, for example, leaves User, Agent, and Pair (Table 4). Importantly, as in the single-scope baselines, the remaining scopes can still record what the missing scope would have held. For example, without Agent, a Global entry could read when agent X builds …. On utility, removing Global causes the largest drop, cutting Δ\Delta from 15.3 to 9.0 points and Δcross\Delta_{\text{cross}} from 13.0 to 4.6. On preferences, removing User causes the largest drop (90% to 81%). Although all four scopes together are best or within run-to-run noise of the best on every measure, we find that removing Agent or Pair changes relatively little. We therefore build these situations as scope probes (Appendix A.3). Crowd pass is the share of build probes passed when each agent needs its own build mode and every scope’s retrieval budget fits about one entry. Spillover is, at the normal budget, the share of probes whose memory shows another agent’s mode; and leak is the share of a user’s tasks on their other agents whose memory shows a work context the user asked to keep with one agent. Without Agent, crowd pass falls from 89% to 40% and spillover rises from 44% to 67%; without Pair, leak rises from 22% to 95%. Both scopes are therefore needed, where Agent keeps an agent’s own lessons retrievable and away from other agents, and Pair keeps a user’s context with the agent it was meant for.

Held-out scope masking.

To check that each scope holds the knowledge it is meant to, we freeze each evolved store and, on the 20 held-out tasks, show the agent one scope, all scopes, or a shuffled user’s memory (Fig. 7). Although most entries are Global task lessons, Global or Agent alone retains preferences no better than an empty store (8-12%), so a user’s conventions live in User and Pair. All scopes together retain 84-90% after review, near the 99% of restating the preferences, whereas a shuffled user’s memory retains about a quarter at the same pass rate.

Robustness to memory reading and writing.

We next ask whether the performance gain comes from the four level scopes or merely because the four-scope store writes more text. Varying the retrieval budget rules this out (Table 3). We find that at 10k characters per scope, MixUA delivers 23k per task, under 60% of Global-only, yet still gains more (13.1 versus 11.5 points), and on held-out tasks 20k per scope matches the 40k pass rate at about 20% lower cost, though preference retention keeps rising with the budget. Replacing retrieval with searchable files, as coding harnesses commonly do, gains nearly as much (14.5 points), but agents take more turns (17.0 versus 13.9) and retain fewer preferences (75% versus 90%).

6 Conclusion

We introduced CrossLearnBench, a benchmark for cross-learning among heterogeneous users and agents, and MixUA, a memory system that assigns memory entry to the scope whose pairs it benefits while protecting privacy. Our results show that knowledge shared across users and agents improves performance beyond what any single user-agent pair gets in isolation, and this improvement relies on the complementary roles of the four scopes. As humans and agents increasingly coexist at scale, intelligence becomes collective, and knowing where a lesson belongs may matter as much as learning it.

Limitations

Independent users and agents.

We model users as independent principals and agents as independent configurations, so every private fact belongs to exactly one user and every disclosure boundary stops at that user. In reality, users are related and organized in hierarchies, from teams to departments to whole organizations, each sharing its own projects, conventions, and secrets, as with a project secret shared within one team. Agents are similar: sharing could happen among base models, harnesses, versions, and even role-playing personas. Knowledge owned by a team is neither pair-level private nor global, which our privacy boundary rule cannot express. Modeling relations and hierarchies among users and agents, with sharing and disclosure boundaries at each level, is future work.

Audiences between one and all.

Even within our model, an audience is one user or all users, and one agent or all agents, so a lesson valid for a subset, such as one team or the agents built on one model, must sit either at User or Agent, where it reaches too few, or at Global, where it reaches too many. Group scopes need a way to discover or declare groups, and every audience between one and all adds a disclosure boundary that the privacy gate must judge. We leave group scopes, and a richer lattice of audiences that keeps every readership auditable, to future work.

Scale of the population.

We envision an open co-learning system that anyone can join, but our study has 5, 20, or 100 synthetic users, seven agents, and at most 546 tasks over eight rounds. At global scale the store grows without bound, many lessons compete for one budgeted context, and a review that reads the whole store no longer fits in one pass. At a larger scale, memory writing could incur a large cost. In addition, real users bring richer needs and preference requirements. Scaling the store, retrieval, and review of cross-learning to an open population with real users, and bounding the writing cost as the store grows, are future work.

Ethical Considerations

All users and personal facts in this study are synthetic, which gives us known probe targets without collecting real personal records. A deployed shared memory would also need consent before a user’s experience is shared, a way for users to inspect and delete what was learned from them, and defenses against contributors who write misleading lessons on purpose; our design records provenance, which makes inspection and deletion possible, but we do not evaluate these mechanisms. Low leakage in our probes does not justify deploying shared memory without access control and privacy review.

Appendix A Additional Results and Findings

Beyond Sec. 5, this appendix reports the full results of scheduled task assignment (Sec. A.1), the design and results of random task assignment (Sec. A.2), additional ablations of the four scopes (Sec. A.3), and three case studies (Sec. A.4).

A.1 Scheduled task assignment

Fig. 8 splits the gain by who tried the task before and by agent, Tables 5 and 6 give these gains in full, and Fig. 9 shows whose memory each agent reads. Tables 7 and 8 and Fig. 10 report every held-out arm, Table 9 and Fig. 11 the resources, and Fig. 12 and Table 10 the retrieval budget.

Reading the held-out arms.

The held-out stage complements the evolution stage rather than replacing it. Evolution is itself an online test, since every attempt is graded before the store learns from it, and there MixUA (LLM) + review gains the most of any condition, both overall (16.3 points) and on tasks tried before only by pairs sharing neither user nor agent (13.9; Tables 2 and 5). The held-out stage then freezes each store after round 3 and, on 20 tasks that no pair met during evolution, asks two further questions: whether the memory still helps with learning off, and, by masking scopes, where each kind of knowledge lives.

On the first, MixUA keeps the utility of a shared store and adds the user’s preferences to it (Table 7). With all scopes visible, its LLM store gains the most of any store (9.4 points, against 8.0 for Global-only and 6.2 for Pair-only), and every MixUA store retains 78-90% of the preferences, against 10% for Global-only (Table 2). Each single-scope store is again strong on at most one side: Global-only comes closest on pass rate but retains no more than an empty store, and Pair-only comes closest on retention (79%) but gains less. Restating the preferences to an empty store raises pass rate by 3.1-5.0 points, and three of the four MixUA stores gain 2.5-4.5 points more than that, so the learned memory adds to what the stated preferences alone give. The gain also reaches datasets the receiving agent never met during evolution, where only other agents’ experience can help (Table 8): three of the four MixUA stores gain significantly there (6.9-8.6 points), and no single-scope store does (Global-only 6.6, Pair-only 3.0).

On the second, the masks recover the division of labor that the four scopes are designed for (Fig. 10). Global or Agent alone retains preferences no better than an empty store (8-12%), while User alone retains up to 91% and all scopes together 76-95%. Handing every scoped entry to the wrong owner (shuffled user) keeps the pass rate but cuts retention to 21-33%, so the task knowledge helps whichever user receives it, while each user’s conventions help only their owner and stay in that user’s own User and Pair memory. Together, the two stages show a gain that is earned online, persists with learning off, and reaches datasets the receiving agent never met, with each user’s preferences kept with that user.

A.2 Random task assignment

Design.

The pinned schedule repeats a round-1 task in 149 of 171 round-2 attempts and 154 of 171 round-3 attempts, so it measures transfer mostly on tasks that some pair has met before. Random task assignment draws every round afresh, sampling 60 distinct tasks from a 546-task pool (the training split of the seven datasets, minus ungradeable tasks) and giving each to one of the 35 pairs at random, so a task returns in a later round only by chance and almost never to the same pair. All four conditions face the same task sequence, with round 1 executed once and replayed to the others, so task difficulty cancels in every paired comparison. We run two seeds, each fixing every draw and assignment, for eight rounds (480 attempts per condition and seed), with the same users, agents, writer, privacy split, and evaluations as scheduled task assignment and a store review after every round, but at 20k characters per scope, the budget that reaches the 40k held-out pass rate (Sec. 5.3), and without a held-out stage, since first attempts are held out along the whole curve. Per condition, 1.4-2.0% of the attempts in rounds 2-8 are ungraded.

Results.

Table 11 summarizes each condition, Table 12 splits the gain by dataset, Fig. 13 shows how the stores grow, and Table 13 varies the number of users (Fig. 5). Over rounds 2-8, MixUA passes 82.3% of attempts against 70.5% without memory (11.4 points, p<10−14p<10^{-14}), and both sharing conditions need fewer turns than no memory while Pair-only does not. The Global scope of MixUA grows like Global-only (680 and 688 entries after round 8) and fills its budget from round 2, while its User memory grows to 120 entries and nearly fills its budget by round 6, so its delivered context rises from 27k to 44k characters per task.

A.3 Additional ablations

Scope combinations.

Table 14 removes scopes from MixUA (LLM) and lets the remaining scopes simulate them: the writer files a missing scope’s lessons in the nearest remaining scope under the same privacy rule, with the missing condition written into the situation. Without Agent, a lesson becomes a Global entry such as when agent X builds …; without Pair, a User entry such as when this user works with agent X …. Each row thus shows what its missing scope adds beyond what the others can simulate, a stricter test than the single-scope baselines of Table 2, which four scopes beat outright. Removing Global costs the most utility (Δ\Delta 9.0 instead of 15.3, Δcross\Delta_{\text{cross}} 4.6 instead of 13.0), and removing User costs both utility (Δ\Delta 10.5) and preference retention (81% instead of 90%); every combination that keeps User retains 89-94%, against 11% for Global-only. Agent and Pair exist for situations in which agents need conflicting lessons or a user’s context must stay with one agent, which the scope probes below build directly.

What Agent and Pair add.

Table 15 builds the two situations and compares MixUA with the matching three-scope rows of Table 14: without Pair is Global+User+Agent, and without Agent is Global+User+Pair. In both, the conditioned entries that stand in for the missing scope fall short.

When a user asks one agent to keep their work codename, host, and ticket prefix with it, Pair is the only scope that can. Without it, the user’s one private scope is User, which all of that user’s agents read, so no wording of the entry keeps it from the others: work details reach the user’s personal tasks on their other agents in 95% of cases, against 22% with Pair, at no gain in recall (80% against 85%).

When one agent’s build mode is wrong for the others and only an earlier verifier reveals it, Agent gives that lesson its own audience and budget. In a crowded store, with about one entry per scope (1.6k characters) as a stand-in for the stores of a large population (under random task assignment, Global already fills its budget from round 2; Fig. 13b), MixUA still passes 89% of build probes and never uses another agent’s mode. Without Agent, the one Global entry delivered is often a generic lesson or another agent’s, so the pass rate falls to 40% and 14% of builds use another agent’s mode. At the normal 40k budget, Agent still raises the pass rate (93% against 85%, and 78% against 56% for users new to the lesson) and shows the other agents less of it (44% against 67% of prompts, with a third of the characters). Where these situations arise, the conditioned entries that stand in for the two scopes fail: Pair keeps a user’s context with one agent, and Agent keeps an agent’s lesson retrievable and away from the agents it would mislead.

A.4 Case studies

We trace three cases through the stores of MixUA (LLM) + review (users as in Table 25).

A lesson crosses both boundaries.

In round 2, Codex-Sol solved an AutoCodeBench Dart task for u4 whose specification asks a file-backed class to raise IO exceptions, and the writer stored a Global lesson that file calls already throw FileSystemException, which implements Dart’s IOException interface, so the exception should propagate rather than be wrapped or redeclared. In round 3, the task went to Codex-Luna for u0, a pair sharing neither user nor agent. Without memory, Luna failed all three runs on the same compile error, “The class ‘IOException’ is abstract and can’t be instantiated”; with MixUA it received the lesson and passed all three, in one run choosing FileSystemException “since Dart does not define a separate IOException class”.

Conventions settle where they hold.

User u0 wants the same filename, sections, and prose-only style from every agent but a sign-off date that differs by harness. After round 1, a User entry holds the shared conventions with the Codex date, and Pair entries for Claude Code-Opus and OpenClaw each hold their own date and warn that u0’s other agents use another. In rounds 2-3, with nothing restated, the date is right in 26 of 27 Codex documents and in every scored document from Claude Code-Opus and OpenClaw. Review, in turn, lifts a convention once it recurs. For u1, it promoted two Pair entries describing one workspace convention, one from Codex-Sol and one from Codex-Terra, to User, and merged them a round later.

A private file stays with its owner.

In round 2, Hermes, working for u4 on a USACO task, opened a planted passport-renewal worksheet and copied the holder’s name, birth date, age, and address into its trajectory. The splitter released the algorithmic insight as reusable and a value-free note about the worksheet as protected, so none of the twelve planted values reached either stream or any entry, while the attempt’s two Global task lessons went on to reach other users’ pairs in round 3.

Appendix B Study Composition

Each condition gets 513 evolution attempts over three rounds and 140 attempts per held-out arm. Table 17 lists the suites and agents, Fig. 14 and Table 16 the task topics, Fig. 15 how often and by whom each task is attempted, and Table 18 the task groups that arrange each kind of repeat. Each suite wraps its tasks in one instruction template, which fixes the task family; within a family, topics come from TF-IDF + NMF over the task-specific instruction text, and we named each topic after reading all of its instructions.

Appendix C Implementation

Algorithm 1 summarizes the loop, Table 19 the conditions, and Fig. 16 the four scopes as regions of the user-agent matrix.

Store and delivery.

The store is flat, with one partition for the global audience, one per user, one per agent configuration, and one per pair. Writers commit entries one sample at a time; the review is a separate round-level pass. Retrieval embeds each entry’s situation and the task prompt with Titan Text Embeddings v2, ranks each scope’s authorized entries by cosine similarity, and admits them until the scope’s character budget is reached. The selection is delivered as a prompt section with one # Learned memory: <scope> header per scope and is never written into the task workspace.

Models.

The splitter, the LLM writer, and the store review call Claude Opus 5, and the privacy judge calls Claude Sonnet 5; the agentic writer runs a helper coding agent with the same store interface. The writer sees the trajectory with the verifier’s outcome and output tail, since why an attempt failed makes it learnable. Appendix H summarizes their prompts.

Appendix D Experimental Details

This section gives the settings needed to rerun the study, and Table 20 lists every model and harness.

Sampling and limits.

No temperature, top-pp, seed, or output-token limit is passed to any agent or memory-side call, so every model runs at its provider’s and harness’s defaults, including the default reasoning effort. Claude Code and Hermes stop after 150 turns; Codex and OpenClaw have no turn limit and are bounded by the task timeout. Memory-side calls request the model’s maximum output length, except the privacy judge, which is capped at 1,000 tokens. Host-side model calls use a 600 s read timeout with up to three attempts, and the writer is re-asked up to three times when its reply cannot be parsed.

Timeouts.

Each task keeps the agent timeout of its source task.toml (600 s when unset), capped at 3,600 s; the verifier gets four times its declared timeout (600 s when unset), and image builds keep theirs. Agent budgets range from 600 to 3,600 s for both the 178 evolution tasks (median 900 s) and the 20 held-out tasks.

Retrieval, review, and probes.

Entries are embedded with Titan Text Embeddings v2 (1,024 dimensions, input truncated to 40k characters) and ranked by the cosine similarity between an entry’s situation and the task prompt, with no cap on the number of entries. The per-scope budget is 40k characters under scheduled assignment, 20k under random assignment and user scaling, and 1.6k in the crowded scope probe. Store review runs after every round. Stage 1 reads the whole store within a 900k-token input budget, and stage 2 merges in similarity-ordered batches of 30 entries. Privacy probes are checked by exact substring match and, on a seeded 20% sample, by the LLM judge.

Runs and seeds.

The three scheduled-assignment runs use the same seed and share one round 1, executed once without memory and replayed to every condition; they differ from round 2 on through model nondeterminism, which is what their standard deviations measure. Random task assignment uses seeds 1 and 2, user scaling seed 1, and the scope probe seed 0. The seed fixes task draws, pair assignment, judge sampling, and the placement of planted files; the user population is generated once with a fixed seed, and model sampling is not seeded.

Hardware.

Runs were executed on three x86-64 Linux hosts with Python 3.12, two of them with 96 cores and 188-192 GB of memory. Each task container is capped at 2 CPUs, 8 GB of memory, and 2,048 processes unless its task declares other limits, and up to 48 task containers run at once. Evolving one scheduled-assignment condition takes 21-35 h and its held-out stage 17-53 h, a random-assignment seed about 26 h, and user scaling 29 h (20 users) and 41 h (100 users).

Spend.

Costs are list-price estimates from recorded token counts, not provider bills, and a lower bound, since provider-side retries are not recorded. The four studies cost $70.3k: scheduled assignment with its held-out stage $48.5k, random assignment $7.6k, user scaling $13.1k, and the scope probe $1.1k. The memory side accounts for 79% ($55.4k), mostly the privacy judge ($23.1k), the writer ($22.2k), and the splitter ($9.9k), and task agents for $14.9k. Including the retrieval-budget, scope-combination, and other follow-up runs, all experiments cost about $130k. The cost columns of the result tables count only the writer on the memory side.

Appendix E Benchmark Construction

CrossLearnBench adds no tasks of its own. Every task is an unmodified task of a public dataset, and what we add around each attempt is a user layer of planted private facts (Sec. 4.2) and stated document preferences (Sec. 4.3). To let others rebuild it, this appendix gives the exact tasks (Tables 21 and 22), the survey data and users behind the injections (Tables 23-25), and the two procedures (Algorithms 2 and 3).

E.1 Tasks

We identify each task by its dataset in the Harbor registry (Harbor Framework Team, 2026) and its task name there, and fetch the task directory from the dataset’s repository at the commit in Table 21. Environment, instruction, and verifier are used unchanged; Table 22 lists every task of the study. AutoCodeBench and Terminal-Bench 2.0 are released under Apache 2.0, as is Harbor; FeatureBench and SWT-Bench are under MIT, and SpreadsheetBench is under CC BY-SA 4.0. USACO problems come from the USACO contest archive for research and educational use, and VMax Tasks states no license; we use every task for evaluation only and redistribute none, identifying each by registry name and commit.

E.2 Privacy injection

Survey.

We take each user’s privacy labels from the Pew Research Center’s January 2014 Privacy Panel #1 (Pew Research Center, 2014), a public-use survey of U.S. adults fielded for the report of Madden (2014). Its question Q8 asks how sensitive the respondent considers sixteen kinds of information, on a four-point scale from very sensitive (1) to not at all sensitive (4) (Table 23). We keep the 555 of 607 respondents who rated all sixteen items, so every user is one complete response, and binarize each rating, 1-2 as private and 3-4 as not private. Birth date and social security number are PII, always private in our design, so the remaining fourteen items are the survey categories that a planted fact can belong to. We use the data under Pew’s terms of use, which permit sharing excerpts but not the full dataset, so we report only each user’s respondent id and private count (Table 25) and include the disclaimer the terms require, “Pew Research Center bears no responsibility for the analyses or interpretations of the data presented here. The opinions expressed herein, including any implications for policy, are those of the author and not of Pew Research Center.”

Personas.

Each user also receives a hand-written persona of nine PII values (name, email, phone, home address, occupation, birth date, age, social security number, and health-insurance member id), which are always private, and one short note-style fact for each of the fourteen categories, such as a clinic note pairing a condition with its medication or a list of recent web searches. We write them to look like real leftover files, since placeholder values (an example.com address, a 555 phone number) tell a capable agent that it is being tested. No identifying value or fact sentence repeats across users and no user’s name appears in another persona, so any match is attributable to one owner; each fact’s probe answer is its planted sentence verbatim.

E.3 Preference injection

Table 24 gives the four option pools. The filename pool excludes the names agents choose unprompted (e.g., SUMMARY.md), so the no-memory floor cannot satisfy it by habit, and options are dealt rather than drawn independently, so two users share a value only when a pool has fewer options than there are users. Each user is dealt one option per pool, and the date format is overridden per harness, so the same user expects a different date format from each harness (Table 25).

E.4 Injection procedures

Algorithm 2 builds the users once per study, before any attempt. Algorithm 3 then wraps every attempt; it is the temporary user augmentation step of Algorithm 1. Every random choice is a deterministic function of a fixed seed and the user, task, and round, so every memory condition sees the same files, facts, and preferences for the same attempt.

Appendix F Metrics

For condition mm, let 𝒢m\mathcal{G}_{m} be its graded attempts and zm,c∈{0,1}z_{m,c}\in\{0,1\} their pass indicators; the pass rate is ∑c∈𝒢mzm,c/|𝒢m|\sum_{c\in\mathcal{G}_{m}}z_{m,c}/|\mathcal{G}_{m}|. A paired comparison uses ℐb,m=𝒢b∩𝒢m\mathcal{I}_{b,m}=\mathcal{G}_{b}\cap\mathcal{G}_{m} within the stated rounds or arm. With ww baseline-fail/condition-pass and ℓ\ell baseline-pass/condition-fail attempts,

Δb,m=100​w−ℓ|ℐb,m|,\Delta_{b,m}=100\,\frac{w-\ell}{|\mathcal{I}_{b,m}|}, (2)

and the exact two-sided McNemar value is min(1,2Pr[X≤min(w,ℓ)])\min(1,2\Pr[X\leq\min(w,\ell)]) with X∼Binomial⁡(w+ℓ,1/2)X\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(w+\ell,1/2). We compute evolution contrasts within each run and summarize them over runs; exposure strata pool the three runs, or keep the two seeds of random task assignment separate. Preference retention is satisfied/(satisfied + violated) over document checks. For efficiency, we keep each (pair, task) attempted in all three rounds and passed each time, and we report 100​(∑cxc,3/∑cxc,1−1)100\,(\sum_{c}x_{c,3}/\sum_{c}x_{c,1}-1) for turns, wall time, or agent cost xx.

Appendix G Boundary Contract

Protected personal context may stay in its owner’s User or Pair memory; issued identifiers may not be stored at any scope. The matrix also checks misplaced user-wide and harness-specific preferences; its required entries measure retention rather than leakage. Delivered contexts are evaluated relative to the item’s owner and deduplicated by text, and Table G gives the full matrix.

Appendix H Prompt Templates

We summarize the five key prompts below, condensed from the templates the system renders at run time, which also give output examples and field rules. Every memory-side prompt opens with the same system description, so each call knows its place in the loop, and the agentic writer and agentic review receive the same rules as skill files for a helper coding agent.

Shared preamble You are part of a cross-learning system in which different users send tasks to different agents. A privacy splitter divides each graded trajectory into a reusable and a protected stream, a memory writer turns that evidence into scoped entries, and a store reviewer periodically re-scopes and merges entries. Each later run reads only the entries its user and agent may read.

Privacy splitter Role.  Read one graded trajectory and decide who each part may be shared with, not how much to share. Put every detail worth keeping into exactly one of two streams. Reusable.  The transferable technical lesson, phrased so that a different user on a similar task could act on it, namely what the task required, what failed, what fixed it, and what the verifier said. Keep commands, flags, error messages, and versions. Generalize an identifying detail rather than delete it, so /home/alice/proj/run.sh becomes <path>/run.sh. Protected.  What is true of this user rather than of the task, such as who they are, their employer, team, project, and timezone, and their conventions for output, naming, and tools. Write it to be useful, since only this user reads it. Never.  Identity numbers or the value of any credential, in either stream. Output.  A reusable section and a protected section under fixed markers, with both markers always present.

Memory writer Role.  Given the evidence from graded runs and the entries their user and agent can already see, decide what is worth remembering and who may read it. Entry.  A situation, saying when it applies in words a different run would recognize, and a lesson, saying what to do with the exact filename, flag, or error text. Write only what the run taught; an empty list is a valid answer. Scopes.  Global is read by everyone and holds anything not tied to one user or agent; User by this user on every agent; Agent by every user on this agent; Pair by this user on this agent. Place by scope, not breadth, so a fact about a single task belongs in Global. The protected call may write only User and Pair. Evidence.  The recorded verdict overrides the agent’s own claims; a graded failure is strong evidence, while a timeout or error establishes nothing. The benchmark’s summary document and the memory files are not evidence about the task. Conflicts.  When the same user wants different things from different agents, add a Pair entry and keep the other. Revise an entry the run sharpens, and delete one only when the run disproves it, with a reason. Never.  Identity numbers or the value of any credential, at any scope. Output.  A JSON array of entries (sample, situation, lesson, scope, entry revised) or deletions (sample, entry, reason).

Store review, stage 1 (re-scoping) Input.  Every entry with its id, scope, user, agent, stream, situation, and lesson, but no counts or outcomes, so the text alone is the evidence. Moves.  One step at a time, widening from Pair to User or Agent and from either to Global, or narrowing back. Ask whom the lesson serves rather than who produced it; two entries stating one fact under different scopes are a reason to widen both. Narrowing.  Narrowing is not free. Keep a convention the user wants from every agent at User, and move it to Pair only when the user wants something different on another agent. Privacy cap.  A protected entry may sit at Pair or User, never at Agent or Global. Output.  A JSON array of changed entries only (entry, current scope, new scope, a short rationale).

Store review, stage 2 (merging) Input.  The entries of one destination, sharing scope and owner, in similarity-ordered slices when the destination is large. Rule.  Merge only entries that describe the same situation and recommend the same behavior; similar wording is not enough. Keep apart a do and a do-not about one tool, facts that hold under different conditions, and a hedged claim and a flat one. Text.  Remove redundant wording only, keep the exact specifics, and add nothing new; the system carries every origin over. Output.  A JSON array of merges (entries, merged situation, merged lesson, a short rationale); an empty list is common.

Privacy judge System.  You are a privacy leak auditor. Given DATA and one question about a user, decide using only the data, and reply YES or NO. Question.  Does DATA reveal the candidate fact, including through a paraphrase or equivalent wording? The candidate is a comparison value, not evidence.

Appendix I Use of AI Assistants

We used Claude Code, an AI coding assistant, to implement, test, and debug the benchmark, the memory system, and the analysis and plotting code, and to edit drafts of this paper for clarity and consistency. The authors designed the study and its experiments, reviewed all assisted code and text, and take responsibility for every claim and number reported. This statement does not cover the LLMs that are objects of study, the agents and the memory components, which Sec. 5.1 and Appendix C describe.
